stemMd:
Ornithologist: Last spring we mounted 200 identical nest boxes in the reserve's oak woodland and 200 in its birch woodland, which is of roughly the same area. Pied flycatchers occupied three times as many of the oak boxes as of the birch boxes. Pied flycatchers therefore prefer oak woodland to birch woodland as a place to nest.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ornithologist's argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Pied flycatchers that cannot find a free nest site in oak woodland will readily settle for a nest site in birch woodland instead.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The nest boxes in both woodlands were of identical design, faced the same direction, and were mounted at the same height above the ground.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Some of the nest boxes in the oak woodland were taken early in the spring by blue tits, which compete with pied flycatchers for nest sites.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Pied flycatchers feed their nestlings chiefly on caterpillars, which are far more abundant on oak leaves than on birch leaves.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The birch woodland already had many natural tree cavities suitable for pied flycatcher nests, whereas the oak woodland had almost none.

explanationMd:
Notice what the evidence measures and what the conclusion claims. The evidence is **box occupancy**. The conclusion is about **preference for a woodland type**. Those come apart whenever birds in one woodland have somewhere else to nest.

The choice describing the birch woodland as already rich in natural tree cavities, with the oak woodland having almost none, supplies exactly that. If the birch woodland is already full of natural cavities and the oak woodland has almost none, then flycatchers nesting in birch had an alternative to the boxes while flycatchers nesting in oak did not. Birch boxes could sit empty in a woodland thick with flycatchers, simply because the birds preferred a real cavity to a wooden box. The occupancy gap is then an artefact of what else was on offer, and tells you nothing about which woodland the birds prefer. The argument is badly damaged.

A useful way to test a weakener is to ask: *does this choice give me a way the premises could all be true while the conclusion is false?* Under that scenario, all 200 birch boxes could be ignored by a large and contented birch population — premises true, conclusion false. No other choice lets you build that story.

Run the same test on the rest. Under the choice about flycatchers settling for birch when oak is unavailable, the birds still go to oak first, which is what preference means. The choice about identical box design, orientation and mounting height removes confounds and so helps the argument. The choice about caterpillar abundance on oak leaves supplies a *reason* for the preference and helps as well. The choice about blue tits taking some of the oak boxes early in the spring mentions a competitor in the oak wood, which if anything means flycatchers took oak boxes despite competition — again not a weakener.

Carry forward the general shape: when a study measures uptake of something researchers provided, always ask what the subjects would have done if the researchers had provided nothing.

distractorRationale.a: This is consistent with the conclusion rather than opposed to it. Saying flycatchers settle for a birch site only when no free oak site is available is close to saying they prefer oak, which is precisely what the ornithologist claims. It is the trap for a reader who registers 'birch' in a positive sentence and reads any mention of the less-used habitat as damaging.
distractorRationale.b: This eliminates confounding differences between the two sets of boxes, in design, orientation and height, and therefore strengthens the argument. A reader can be drawn to it because controls feel like the sort of methodological detail that turns up in an objection, but the direction of the effect here is plainly supportive.
distractorRationale.d: This offers a mechanism, a richer food supply for nestlings, that would explain a genuine preference for oak, so it supports the conclusion rather than undermining it. It tempts anyone who selects the choice that introduces the most new biology without first asking which way the new fact cuts.
distractorRationale.c: If blue tits took some oak boxes early in the spring, fewer oak boxes were left for flycatchers, yet flycatchers still occupied three times as many oak boxes as birch ones. That makes the gap harder to achieve, not easier to explain away. The choice is attractive because it complicates the oak figure, but complicating a figure in the direction that makes the result harder to achieve cannot weaken the conclusion.

accessibilityText: A short argument from an ornithologist. Two hundred identical nest boxes were placed in oak woodland and two hundred in birch woodland of roughly equal area; pied flycatchers occupied three times as many oak boxes as birch boxes; the ornithologist concludes that the birds prefer oak woodland for nesting. The question asks which statement, if true, most weakens the argument. Five answer choices, labelled A through E. No notation, tables or figures appear.

provenance.notes: Original stimulus and choices. Weaken item in which the measured proxy (uptake of a resource supplied by the researchers) diverges from the conclusion's subject (habitat preference) because of an unmeasured alternative resource. Not derived from any published LSAT item.

review.author: lsat-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: If birch woodland already had many natural cavities while oak had almost none, flycatchers in birch had little need for boxes, so box occupancy measures scarcity of nest sites rather than preference between woodlands. Identical box design and caterpillar abundance on oak strengthen the argument; blue tits taking oak boxes would lower oak occupancy, making the observed gap more striking; fallback settling in birch when oak is full is consistent with an oak preference. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: If the birch woodland already had many natural cavities while the oak had almost none, flycatchers in birch had less need of boxes, so lower box occupancy there does not show a preference for oak woodland. Settling for birch only when oak is full implies oak is preferred (strengthens); blue tits taking oak boxes means the oak figure understates flycatcher interest (strengthens); caterpillar abundance on oak gives a reason for preference; identical box design removes a confound (strengthens).]

review.notes: Author solved the item and then tried to argue each other choice as a weakener; the choices about settling for birch, identical boxes, blue tits and caterpillars are all neutral or supportive. 'Of roughly the same area' was added to the stimulus deliberately so that no choice about relative habitat extent could serve as a second weakener. Awaiting blind independent solve. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key. v2 (2026-09-24): corrected 3 option references in the explanation that still used the option order from before the options were reordered (the explanation pointed to a wrong option as the answer, or discussed the answer under a wrong letter). Letters in the notes above may use the old order. Correction by the coordinating editor (an AI agent), checked mechanically against the stored option order and the original order of the distractor notes; a separate AI reviewer re-checked every option reference against the option text, and the item passed a new blind solve on 2026-09-24. v1 stays attached to earlier attempts. Option-letter references in the explanation were rewritten to name choice content; the key was re-derived independently and is unchanged. Version 3 merges the letter-free wording of the choices with version 2's review; the key and the choices are unchanged. Choices rebalanced on 2026-09-29 to remove an answer-length cue; the key is unchanged.
